digest.intro: Institutions cracking, bodies learning to move, and languages nobody can read.

items.title: The Iran War Reignites — What Actually Happened on July 29
items.blurb: CENTCOM launched its largest strike wave against the IRGC since February — hitting command centers, missile facilities, and naval assets — after Iran used a 72-hour diplomatic lull to reload its launchers. The same 24-hour window saw Saudi Arabia conduct its first acknowledged offensive strikes and call for a Red Sea naval coalition, a Russian cruise missile cross Polish airspace, and China tighten its maritime encirclement of Taiwan from the east. This is the most organized single summary of what's actually moving right now.

items.title: UEFA's 55 Associations Threaten to Walk — the Kushner–FIFA Deal Explained
items.blurb: Infantino's plan to sell 20% of the World Cup to Joshua Kushner's private equity fund has triggered the most serious institutional split in global football in decades, with all 55 UEFA national associations threatening collective boycott. The web: Charles Kushner (convicted of tax evasion and witness tampering, pardoned by Trump) is now U.S. ambassador to France despite speaking no French; brother Joshua runs the fund; FIFA is renting office space in Trump Tower. The House Judiciary Committee's Jamie Raskin called it a "kickback hat-trick."

items.title: Hamas Disarmament Deal — What's Being Claimed
items.blurb: Trump announced a deal for complete Hamas disarmament with Israeli withdrawal — if real, the most significant Middle East development of 2026. Heavy conditions remain unresolved and the sourcing is thin, but it's the story today and worth tracking rather than ignoring.

items.title: Gemini Robotics 2: Whole-Body Intelligence
items.blurb: DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2 moves past arm-only manipulation into full-body coordination — crouch, stretch, walk, manipulate, hand off to another robot — and can run on-device while transferring learned skills to entirely different robot morphologies. The shift from pre-programmed narrow sequences to adaptive whole-body reasoning is the conceptual jump here: the robot body stops being a fixed tool and starts being a substrate the intelligence can inhabit. Relevant if you think about physical making at any scale.

items.title: The Session You Cannot Take With You
items.blurb: A sharp piece on how AI inference APIs are quietly destroying the property that made them interoperable: the portable transcript. Reasoning tokens are billed to you but returned as encrypted blobs; web searches show the model source material you never see; compacted context is locked to the original provider. The argument is that each of these features has a plausible individual justification while the aggregate effect is deliberate vendor lock-in dressed as technical necessity.

items.title: Montana Opens a Legal Pathway to Sell Experimental Drugs Directly to Patients
items.blurb: Montana just finalized rules allowing biotech companies to sell experimental treatments — sometimes tested in as few as 10 healthy people — to any consenting adult who can pay, with a $12,500 application fee to a state review board. Unlike other right-to-try laws, this isn't limited to terminal illness; longevity and preventive therapies are explicitly in scope. The first experimental treatment clinics are expected to open by end of 2026, which makes this an institutional experiment as much as a medical one.

items.title: New African Masquerades: Costume as Living Identity Technology
items.blurb: An upcoming MFA St. Petersburg exhibition brings together four contemporary West African artists — from Nigeria, Burkina Faso, Sierra Leone, and Cameroon — who are actively mutating the masquerade tradition: geometric masks in bold pigment, costumes from dyed fiber, pop culture references embedded in sacred forms. The masquerade is one of the oldest human answers to the question of how a community makes contact with something beyond itself, and these artists are treating it as a live medium rather than an archive. David Sanou's geometric ensembles and Hervé Youmbi's work in particular look worth finding.

facts.fact: Charles Kushner — convicted of tax evasion, witness tampering, and illegal campaign contributions — is currently the U.S. ambassador to France, despite speaking no French.

Montana's new right-to-try law allows experimental drugs tested in as few as 10 healthy people to be sold to any consenting adult — not just the terminally ill — for a $12,500 review board application fee.

Adult black-and-white ruffed lemurs have been documented choosing to playfight with juvenile ring-tailed lemurs over available members of their own species — the first recorded instance of this interspecific play between the two.

Cheap H96 streaming sticks running a backdoor by Zhejiang Fengwo IoT impersonate Samsung, Huawei, and Xiaomi phones to fraudulently click ads on AI-generated websites — discovered when a researcher registered an expired coordination domain and watched tens of thousands of devices check in.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film that functions as a memory machine — Marker stitches together Tokyo, Guinea-Bissau, and Iceland into something that asks how images store experience and whether any of it is real. Obsessive, deeply personal, and structurally unlike anything else; a direct ancestor of the essay-film form and the kind of work that makes you want to rebuild your entire practice.

art_picks.title: Pace Gallery: Paul Thek
art_picks.creator: Paul Thek
art_picks.why: Thek spent his career making work that collapsed the boundaries between sculpture, installation, ritual, and painting — deeply strange objects that sit at the intersection of the corporeal and the symbolic. His rarely-seen later works are exactly the kind of obsessive, category-refusing practice that rewards going deep.

art_picks.title: Music Has the Right to Children
art_picks.creator: Boards of Canada
art_picks.why: If you want something that sounds like half-remembered childhood encoded in synthesis — warm, uncanny, with internal logic so tight it feels like a discovered system rather than composed music. The whole record operates as a kind of memory architecture, which rhymes directly with how you think about generative space.

events.name: Made in America: The Industrial Photography of Christopher Payne
events.venue: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, 2 East 91st Street, Manhattan
events.why: 70+ large-format photographs of American factories — Payne went obsessively deep into the hidden systems of making, from marshmallow production lines to Giant Magellan Telescope components; a meditation on craft, labor, and the aesthetics of industrial process that's more compelling in person at scale.

events.name: Whitney Biennial 2026
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort Street, Manhattan
events.why: The 82nd edition foregrounds mood and texture over thesis — 56 artists exploring technological affinities, shared mythologies, and infrastructural networks, with a notable thread of subversive cuteness smuggling in critique; worth it for the few genuinely strange installations before it closes.

events.name: Greater New York 2026
events.venue: MoMA PS1, 22-25 Jackson Avenue, Long Island City, Queens
events.why: A building-wide, free quinquennial survey of 53 NYC-based artists — site-specific commissions, animation, scenography, and new productions tracking surveillance, economic precarity, and shifting tech; exactly the kind of show where social systems are visible before they harden.

events.name: Gabriel Orozco: Public Nature
events.venue: JCDecaux Bus Shelters, New York City (citywide)
events.why: Orozco turns bus shelter ad panels into site-specific photographs of urban ephemera — found objects, chance encounters, sculptural interventions embedded in the city's actual infrastructure; a commission that makes the city itself the gallery.

events.name: NoMad Jazz Festival 2026
events.venue: Madison Square Park & NoMad neighborhood venues, Manhattan
events.why: A week of free pop-up jazz performances woven into restaurants, retail, and public spaces across a neighborhood — jazz as community infrastructure, culminating in free mainstage concerts in Madison Square Park on Aug 7–8 with José James and Ben Wendel among the headliners.
